title: Type conversions: intent, information loss, and range checks
lead: Identify an operation’s type before it runs and use static_cast only with a justified intention.
why: An explicit cast can look convincing while neither checking bounds nor restoring a lost fraction. We examine repairs that must occur earlier and warnings that require reasoning.
objectives: Distinguish implicit conversion, promotion, and explicit static_cast.
Obtain fractional division by converting an operand before /.
Explain the selected mixed-sign example and unsigned modulo.
Check valid ranges before a potentially lossy conversion.
Use narrowing diagnostics as useful evidence.
prerequisites: Integer division, ranges, long long, and intermediate values.
bool and simple comparisons from the laboratory; a protective if is scaffolded.

concepts.definition: Conversion to a required type without an explicit cast in source.
Promotion of a small integer type to int or unsigned int according to representability.
An explicit permitted conversion to T, not a universal safety check.
A conversion risking range or precision loss; list initialization rejects specified cases.
Unsigned-value behavior modulo two raised to the type’s width.

sections.title: Session 1. The common type is chosen before the operation
paragraphs: With two ints, total / count performs integer division. Storing the result in double afterward cannot restore the fraction. static_cast<double>(total / count) first obtains integer 3 and then double 3.0; static_cast<double>(total) / count converts an operand first and gives 3.5 for 7 and 2.

In static_cast<double>(total), static_cast selects an explicit conversion, <double> specifies the destination type, and parentheses contain the expression. It is a language operator rather than a function we authored. Use it to state justified intent; unnecessary casts can obscure meaning.

sections.title: Promotions and usual arithmetic conversions
paragraphs: Before many integer operations, bool, char, and short undergo integral promotions: to int when it represents all source values, otherwise to unsigned int. Thus adding two chars does not necessarily yield char. Type rules, not the length of the printed number, determine the result.

After promotions, arithmetic operators choose a common type. In our double-and-int examples the integer operand converts to double. Same-sign integer types convert toward the greater rank; mixed signs need additional rules. Rank is a language ordering rather than merely sizeof. Do not replace the rules with “the larger size always wins.”

sections.title: Why −1 < 1u can be false
paragraphs: In this example debt is int and credit is unsigned int. Their ranks correspond, so int converts to unsigned int before comparison. −1 becomes the maximum unsigned int value and comparison with 1 is false. This follows defined conversion rules rather than a compiler defect.

Unsigned integer conversion is congruent modulo 2^N, where N is the destination width. We do not assume N=32 universally. The example compares with numeric_limits<unsigned int>::max() instead of demanding one numeric maximum. Repairing a domain comparison requires valid signs and ranges rather than blindly casting both sides to unsigned.

sections.title: Session 2. static_cast is not a validator
paragraphs: Converting double 3.75 to int gives 3, and −3.75 gives −3: the fraction is discarded toward zero rather than rounded to the nearest integer. We execute only values whose truncated result is representable. Out-of-range floating-to-integer conversion is not a safe experiment.

Before narrowing, establish the destination range and domain rules. If a value must be a whole count, losing a fraction can be wrong even within range. static_cast does not automatically reject that domain error. int count{2.5}; usefully detects specified narrowing during the build; do not add a cast merely to silence it.

sections.title: Change the type before information is lost
paragraphs: Widening before multiplication and converting before division solve the same design problem: choosing operation semantics before execution. Casting an already-overflowed or truncated result cannot repair the past.

Keep exact totals in integer minor units and calculate an approximate average separately. This distinguishes exact stored quantities from derived approximations. If every cent matters, formatting and rounding must be explicit contract rules rather than accidental cast consequences.

sections.title: Verification and practicum B
paragraphs: For the average, test 7/2, 0/2, 10/4, and rejection of zero count. The first and third expose premature integer division; zero alone cannot. Write expected values 3.5, 0, and 2.5 before running.

Practicum B combines named stages, integer-product bounds, and a floating-point average. Reference values allow simple output; full formatting is introduced in lesson 12. The diagram compares two specific division paths rather than executing arbitrary C++ conversions.

diagnostics.cause: Two integers were divided before converting the result.
diagnostics.fix: Convert an operand before / and repeat a nonmultiple case.

diagnostics.symptom: A negative value became very large
diagnostics.fix: Inspect the common type and domain range rather than hiding a warning with a guessed cast.

diagnostics.symptom: Narrowing diagnostic vanished but meaning was lost
diagnostics.cause: An explicit cast was added without deciding whether fraction loss was valid.
diagnostics.fix: Establish the contract and bounds before converting.
